title: Neighbor-independent substitution systems cannot emulate cellular automata

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Neighbor-independent substitution systems cannot emulate cellular automata

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Neighbor-independent substitution systems can only generate repetitive or nested patterns, so they cannot emulate cellular automata such as rule 30, whereas neighbor-dependent substitution systems can emulate cellular automata straightforwardly.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: For as we discussed on page 83, neighbor-independent substitution systems can generate only patterns that are either repetitive or nested—so they can never yield the more complicated patterns that are, for example, needed to emulate rule 30.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 11, “The Notion of Computation”; section “Emulating Cellular Automata with Other Systems” (from p. 664), p. 666. Scope: neighbor-independent and neighbor-dependent substitution systems

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch11-09: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.85

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The constructive neighbor-dependent part is straightforward. The independent-substitution limitation is provable under a formalized direct-emulation notion, although the informal pattern vocabulary lowers operationalizability.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Characterize words generated by independent symbol substitutions and prove their structural closure, then test whether a fixed local decoding can reproduce rule 30 spacetime behavior. Separately construct the direct neighbor-dependent substitution encoding of a cellular-automaton update.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Impossibility varies with the allowed encoding and time rescaling.

'Nested' needs a formal language-theoretic definition.

data existence: 0.9

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The evolution diagram of a neighbor-independent substitution system is produced by uniform replacement, so its nested or ultimately repetitive form is a structural theorem, and rule 30's diagram is not of that form. The neighbor-dependent direction is an explicit, small construction that can be checked step by step. Both directions are within a short proof or a short program.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Treat a neighbor-independent substitution system as iteration of a fixed morphism and show that its evolution diagram is self-similar by construction, hence repetitive or nested, and therefore not the evolution of rule 30. Separately, implement the neighbor-dependent construction and check that it reproduces rule 90 and rule 30. A non-nested neighbor-independent diagram would refute the first half; a failed copy would refute the second.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value: Nested has to be read as the self-similar geometry of morphism iteration; a claim about every scalar sequence derived from such a system would be broader than the evolution diagram.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

analysis feasibility: 0.8
operationalizability: 0.85
data adequacy: 0.85
discriminating power: 0.85

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: If the claim holds, every neighbour-independent substitution system in a complete enumerated family (2 colours with replacement blocks of length 1-3; 3 colours with blocks of length 1-2) produces, from a single cell, a sequence whose subword complexity stays bounded (repetitive) or grows at most polynomially slowly (nested), far below the near-exponential subword complexity of rule 30's rows and centre column, so none of them can reproduce rule 30; while a neighbour-dependent substitution system (one output cell per cell, chosen from the cell and its two neighbours) reproduces rules 90 and 30 exactly.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py enumerates all 196 two-colour (blocks 1-3) and 1728 three-colour (blocks 1-2) neighbour-independent substitution rules, iterates each from a single cell of colour 1 until the word has 131072 symbols (or 60 steps), and counts distinct factors of length 1..14 with a sorted rolling-code method. It generates rule 30 from a single black cell with big-integer bit operations, taking the central 40001 cells of row 20000 and the first 65536 centre-column cells, and applies the same count. It also measures what share of the centre column's length-14 factors appear in any binary substitution word, and runs the one-cell-per-cell neighbour-dependent substitution systems for rules 90 and 30 against the direct CA for 1000 steps. Runtime about 19 s.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. For each of the 196 two-colour rules {0 -> w0, 1 -> w1} with |w0|, |w1| in {1,2,3} and each of the 1728 three-colour rules with block lengths in {1,2}, start from a single cell of colour 1 and iterate until the word has >= L = 131072 symbols (or 60 steps if it never does), truncate to L, and compute the number p(n) of distinct length-n factors for n = 1..14. For rule 30 from a single black cell compute p(14) of (i) the central 40001 cells of the row at step 20000 and (ii) the first 65536 cells of the centre column. Build the neighbour-dependent substitution system whose rule maps each cell to one new cell given by the elementary-CA table of its (left, self, right) neighbourhood, and run it for 1000 steps from a single black cell. PASS (supports) if (a) every neighbour-independent rule has p(14) <= 225 = (14+1)^2 (eventually periodic words are those with p(14) = p(13); the rest are counted as nested), (b) both rule 30 sequences have p(14) >= 2000, and (c) the neighbour-dependent systems for rules 90 and 30 reproduce the cellular-automaton rows exactly at every one of the 1000 steps.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. FAIL (refutes) if any neighbour-independent rule in the family has p(14) >= 2000 (rule-30-like complexity), or if the neighbour-dependent construction does not reproduce rule 90 or rule 30. If some neighbour-independent rule has 225 < p(14) < 2000 the result is 'mixed' and the rule is reported with its complexity profile.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: maximum number of distinct length-14 factors over all 1924 neighbour-independent substitution words (threshold 225)

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: 'Repetitive' is operationalised as eventually periodic (bounded subword complexity, Morse-Hedlund), 'nested' as a self-similar word, which for fixed points of morphisms has subword complexity O(n^2) at most (Pansiot); the threshold (n+1)^2 at n = 14 is therefore a generous upper bound for repetitive-or-nested and about a tenth of what a random-like binary sequence of this length shows. 'Cannot emulate rule 30' is tested within the enumerated family by the complexity gap (a word with p(14) <= 225 cannot contain the rule 30 row, whose own p(14) is measured); it is not a proof over all encodings. The neighbour-dependent half is tested exactly as the book describes it (rules 'always yielding just one cell and corresponding quite directly to cellular automata', p. 666).

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value: Enumerated neighbour-independent substitution systems (2 colours, blocks 1-3; 3 colours, blocks 1-2), rule 30 evolutions, and neighbour-dependent substitution emulations of rules 90 and 30, generated by analysis.py

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
The impossibility half is tested on the two complete enumerated families named in the book's own discussion (p. 83), not for arbitrarily long replacement blocks or alphabets; the complexity gap (at most 157 distinct length-14 factors versus 14922-16034 for rule 30) is a finite proxy for the theorem that fixed points of morphisms have polynomially bounded subword complexity.

The subword-complexity criterion treats any word with p(14) <= 225 as repetitive-or-nested; the words with the largest complexity (e.g. 0 -> 0, 1 -> 011, p(n) = 2,4,6,9,13,...,81) are non-primitive morphic words whose complexity grows faster than linearly but far below that of rule 30, consistent with the known n log n / n^2 classes for such words.

The neighbour-dependent half is near-definitional: a substitution system whose single output cell depends on the cell and its two neighbours is a cellular automaton; the test confirms it reproduces rules 90 and 30 exactly for 1000 steps, which is what the book's figure shows.

The length-14 factor share result (at most 0.5% of rule 30's centre-column factors occur in any binary substitution word) is reported as a direct check that none of the enumerated systems reproduces rule 30's sequence under the identity encoding; other encodings were not explored.
